title: West of the Glass Hills
summary: A county mapmaker has until six to finish her western line. A young traveling storyteller brings her a letter the post office keeps returning. Following six picture cards to a moving market, they discover why one place can need two names—and why another needs a date.
coverAlt: A wide Western landscape in indigo, ochre and vermilion stretches around a cartographer with a black braid, a young storyteller holding picture cards, and their ash-gray mule. The setting sun lights the glassy terraces behind the title.
style: Western travel-poster lithography with cut-block silhouettes, indigo cliff shadows, ochre grasses and vermilion accents. Two illustrated panels run from left to right across each broad landscape page.

pages.alt: Beside the printshop’s press, Sol shows Mara a broad unfinished map. Mara spreads the sheet flat and studies the open space beyond its blue lines.
pages.transcript:
Sol: Six o’clock, Mara. After the bell, the first hundred sheets go under the roller.
Mara: There’s half a county west of this blue line. Why does the plate leave it blank?

pages.alt: At the post-office counter, Teo and the clerk hold opposite ends of a returned envelope. Outside, he shows its picture of two peaks to Mara, with his route cards fanned below.
pages.transcript:
Teo: My aunt Eda has a stall at Two Shadows. The post office has sent this back twice.
Mara: Come and show me. I have until six to put a place on that plate.

pages.alt: Ash-gray mule in tow, Mara and Teo walk west between terraced mesas. Teo fans his illustrated route cards beside Mara’s folded map.
pages.transcript:
Teo: I carry my whole route in six pictures. People remember a story longer than a number.
Mara: My map has numbers. We’ll see which of us gets lost first.

pages.alt: Mara looks toward a pair of distant stone needles. At a fork, Teo points to the kettle on his card and turns toward the willow-lined bend.
pages.transcript:
Mara: Two Shadows! Those two stone needles must be it.
Teo: Then the next picture should be a mountain. Mine is a kettle.

pages.alt: A kettle hangs beside the ferry while Mara and Teo meet the ferrymaker and her neighbors. The ferrymaker taps the copper pot as Teo holds up his matching picture.
pages.transcript:
Ferrymaker: Kettle Bend. Before we had a bell, Gran called the ferry with her soup pot.
Mara: My sheet calls it West Crossing. Would a driver looking for Kettle Bend ever stop?

pages.alt: Mara marks the river crossing on her sheet. By the ferry, Teo listens to local directions and makes a note on a card.
pages.transcript:
Ferrymaker: Keep West Crossing too. My brother sends parcels there. Both names find us.
Teo: Two names at one stop. That’s going to be a crowded little map.

pages.alt: The travelers approach a blue bench painted with yellow flowers. The smiling wagon driver and Teo sit together under a tree with his cards and a tin cup.
pages.transcript:
Wagon driver: Two Shadows? I was there on weaving day. Ask again before you draw a dot.
Mara: Weaving day? I can measure a hillside. How do I measure a Thursday?

pages.alt: Mara checks the time at a fork in the road. Her hand and Teo’s point to different routes on a map laid over a rock.
pages.transcript:
Mara: The coach road gets my plate back by six. The lower road takes us to your aunt.
Teo: If we go back now, you can copy the names. You still won’t know where my letter goes.

pages.alt: Mara tucks her watch away while holding the survey map. The travelers and their laden mule take the winding lower road toward a distant market.
pages.transcript:
Mara: I gave Sol my word. I also put my name on every line. We take the lower road.
Teo: Good. The best part of a story always happens off the short way.

pages.alt: Two broad blue awnings shade the looms and stalls at a busy weaving market. Teo points down between their joining shadows while Mara looks at the ground.
pages.transcript:
Eda: You took your time, Teo! Set that letter in the cool, between my two awnings.
Mara: Two Shadows. I spent the morning looking up. I should have been looking down.

pages.alt: Teo hands an envelope to Eda at her loom. Eda unties a small white bundle while Teo points to the open spot in her bright woven cloth.
pages.transcript:
Teo: It’s the moth block you left at our house. You said your big cloth needed one last wing.
Eda: Tomorrow I could have woven a different wing. I wanted this one.

pages.alt: Mara bends over her map as Eda gestures across the steps, awnings and trading stalls. Beside a folded awning on a cart, Eda points down the valley to another settlement.
pages.transcript:
Mara: I’ll put Two Shadows here, beside the bench. No more returned letters.
Eda: Careful. Next month our market moves. Pin the tents down and your fine map tells a lie.

pages.alt: Teo scratches the back of his head as he looks at a card beside Mara. Eda and the other travelers point out the ferry, bench and tents together on a large map.
pages.transcript:
Teo: I called this fork Teo’s Turn once. It made a grand ending. Nobody else called it that.
Mara: Then ask whose ending it was. Eda, where do people ask when the market moves?

pages.alt: Mara inks the river line while Eda points toward the ferry. Teo and Mara arrange printing blocks showing a kettle, a bench, an awning and a calendar.
pages.transcript:
Eda: The ferry keeps a market list. The driver at the bench knows the next stop too.
Mara: A fixed line for the road. Two names for the ferry. A dated sign for a moving place.

pages.alt: The travelers see the glowing printshop windows below the hill at twilight. Sol stands beside the press and a stack of maps as Mara returns.
pages.transcript:
Teo: There goes six.
Sol: Twenty sheets printed. Eighty waiting. What did you bring that couldn’t wait for morning?

pages.alt: Mara positions a strip of new symbols over the signature space on the county map. Sol holds up the sheet with its big round signature frame as Mara points into the empty space.
pages.transcript:
Mara: You saved me a whole corner for my signature. Put the ferry names and market sign there.
Sol: You waited six years to sign a county sheet. You mean to give that space away?

pages.alt: Mara signs beside the edge of the map. Sol and Mara work a second color into an already-printed sheet on the press.
pages.transcript:
Mara: The edge will hold my name. The middle ought to hold the people who live there.
Sol: A second pass in red. Even those first twenty sheets can carry it.

pages.alt: At the post counter the clerk and Teo study the freshly printed county map. Mara leans across the sheet with two red stamps while the clerk traces the map key and Teo holds another sealed envelope.
pages.transcript:
Clerk: This tells me where the tents were. Where do I send something next month?
Mara: Read the red key aloud. This time, if you stumble, the map has to change.

pages.alt: The clerk hands the sealed envelope across a ferry stall marked with a kettle and a calendar. The wagon driver passes an envelope to Eda at the market, with Teo looking on.
pages.transcript:
Clerk: Kettle Bend, also West Crossing. Ask here for this month’s Two Shadows. I can do that.
Eda: A letter that found me first try. That is a handsome sort of map.

pages.alt: A girl with two dark braids runs up the road after Mara, Teo and their mule. At a low stone wall, Teo offers the girl a blank card while Mara opens her map.
pages.transcript:
Child: There’s a place past this hill. My father has a name for it, and I have another.
Teo: Then start with yours. We’ve got room for both.
